claims.claim: Databricks Free Edition offers serverless compute only.

concept_html:
Track A uses a handful of Databricks words on every page. This lesson places each one.

Workspace, notebooks, compute, jobs. You work in a workspace, writing code in notebooks. Code runs on compute: serverless compute that Databricks manages for you, or a cluster you configure. Databricks Free Edition offers serverless compute only. A job runs notebooks on a schedule, with parameters (lesson A10-L2).

Unity Catalog organises data and permissions with three-level names, catalog.schema.table:

  • a catalog per environment, such as research_dev and research_prod,
  • a schema per layer, such as research_silver,
  • a table, such as nat_respondents.

Volumes hold files, such as raw delivery CSVs, under the same names and permissions. Grants go to groups, never to individual users (lesson A4-L2).

Delta tables. A table created USING DELTA, the Databricks default, is a folder of Parquet data files plus a transaction log, _delta_log. Each write adds one numbered JSON commit to the log, so the table has versions 0, 1, 2 and so on. DESCRIBE HISTORY t lists them, and SELECT * FROM t VERSION AS OF 1 reads an older one (lesson A3-L3). Readers never see a half-finished write.

Medallion layers give each table one job:

  • Bronze keeps every delivery as received, plus audit columns: nat_raw.
  • Silver has clean names and types and one row per respondent per wave: nat_respondents.
  • Gold holds business-ready aggregates with a stated grain: nat_metrics.

Data moves forward only. A fix in silver logic means rebuilding silver from bronze, never editing bronze. Module A2 sets the contract for each layer.

Raise `ValueError` naming the input when there are not exactly three parts, or when any part is empty.
exercises.prompt_html: Write parse_table_name(name: str) -> tuple[str, str, str] for a job that must only ever write to fully named tables. Split the name on dots and return (catalog, schema, table). Raise ValueError naming the input when there are not exactly three parts, or when any part is empty.
exercises.solution:
def parse_table_name(name: str) -> tuple[str, str, str]:
    """Split a Unity Catalog table name into catalog, schema and table.

    Args:
        name: A name such as research_prod.research_silver.nat_respondents.

    Returns:
        (catalog, schema, table).

    Raises:
        ValueError: If the name does not have exactly three non-empty parts.
    """
    parts = name.split(".")
    if len(parts) != 3 or any(part == "" for part in parts):
        raise ValueError(f"expected catalog.schema.table, got {name!r}")
    catalog, schema, table = parts
    return catalog, schema, table

title: The lakehouse map, Databricks, Unity Catalog, Delta and medallion layers
why_html: Two analysts both wrote to a table called respondents, one in the development catalog and one in production, because their notebooks used two-part names and different default catalogs. Production silver received a week of test rows before anyone noticed. Three-level names, with the catalog stated explicitly or set from a job parameter, make the target impossible to mistake.
